lead: Today's readings set two kinds of wealth side by side. Paul tells Timothy to warn the rich not to trust in uncertain riches but to be “rich in good works”. In the Gospel, a woman known as a sinner pours out costly ointment and tears on the feet of Jesus, and is called rich in love. The true treasure is a heart that has received much and gives much.

set: 1 Timothy is one of the three Pastoral Letters, addressed to Timothy, Paul's companion, who was caring for the church at Ephesus. Earlier in this chapter the letter warns that “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (6:10). Now, near the end, it turns to those in the community who are already rich, and does not condemn them but gives them a task.
str: v. 17: two warnings (do not be haughty; do not hope in riches) and the right hope: God, who richly provides.
v. 18: four positive commands: do good, be rich in good works, be generous, share.
v. 19: the result: a good foundation for the future, and “the life that really is life”.
kw: The letter speaks of the rich “in the present age”: their riches belong to a world that is passing.
From koinōnia, communion. Sharing goods is a form of the fellowship of the Church (compare Acts 2:44–45).
the life that really is life
Literally “the real life”. Wealth gives a kind of life; God gives the life that is truly life.
vv: As for those who in the present age are rich, command them not to be haughty, or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but rather on God who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment.
Notice the last words: God gives us things “for our enjoyment”. The letter does not despise created goods; it puts them in their place.
They are to do good, to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share,
so that they may take hold of the life that really is life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the owner of goods is a steward of Providence, who should make them bear fruit and share the benefits with others, first of all his family (CCC 2404). It quotes St John Chrysostom: “Not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life” (CCC 2446).

set: This scene is found only in Luke. Jesus has just been called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (7:34), and now we see what that means. A Pharisee named Simon invites him to a meal. Luke shows Jesus at table with Pharisees several times (11:37; 14:1), and the meal becomes a lesson for the host.
str: vv. 36–38: the woman's act at Jesus' feet.
vv. 40–43: the parable of two debtors.
vv. 44–46: three contrasts: water, kiss, oil.
v. 47: her many sins forgiven; little forgiveness, little love.
vv. 48–50: “Your sins are forgiven … Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
kw: Luke does not tell us her sin, and he does not give her a name. She is known by her love.
A labourer's wage for one day (Matthew 20:2). The two debts are about a year and a half's wages, and less than two months'.

The little word hoti can give the reason (“because”) or the evidence (“which shows that”). The NRSV reads “hence she has shown great love”, following the parable, where love comes from forgiveness; the Malayalam POC reads “because she loved much”. Catholic interpreters hold both: love is the fruit of forgiveness received, and love opens the heart to receive it.
vv: She stood behind him at his feet, weeping, and began to bathe his feet with her tears and to dry them with her hair.
Guests reclined on low couches with their feet stretched out behind them, so she could reach his feet without coming to the table. Every gesture is a gesture of love: tears, hair, kisses, ointment.
Simon has seen only “a sinner” (v. 39). Jesus asks him to see a person.
Therefore, I tell you, her sins, which were many, have been forgiven; hence she has shown great love. But the one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.
Your faith has saved you; go in peace.
The same words Jesus speaks to the woman healed of bleeding (8:48). Faith receives; peace is the gift.
ch: The Catechism teaches that only God forgives sins, and that Jesus, as Son of God, exercises this divine power and gives it to his Church (CCC 1441–1442). The guests' question, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” (v. 49), is the right question. Pope St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, saw in the woman's tears the model of a penitent who turns all that once served sin into the service of God (in substance).

qa: Luke does not say so. He introduces Mary Magdalene separately in the next chapter (8:2). In the West, from the time of St Gregory the Great, the two were often identified; the Eastern tradition has generally kept them distinct. The Church does not require either view; the Gospel's point is her love and her forgiveness.
study: Paul tells the rich to be “rich in good works”. What could I share this week, of money, time or skill?
Simon saw “a sinner”; Jesus saw a woman who loved. Whom do I need to see with the eyes of Jesus?
